alignment.note: The Vulgate transmits an entirely different verse (Mark 9:8: 'And immediately looking around, they saw no one anymore except Jesus alone with them'), whereas the Greek and Peshitta attest Mark 9:7 (the divine voice from the cloud). This represents a critical textual displacement or versification error in the supplied Vulgate witness.

Greek uses a present participle with dative object (ἐπισκιάζουσα αὐτοῖς, 'overshadowing them'); Peshitta employs a finite verb construction with prepositional phrase (ܘܡܛܠܐ ܗܘܬ ܥܠܝܗܘܢ, 'and it was overshadowing upon them'), semantically equivalent but syntactically distinct.

Greek repeats the conjunction and verb (καὶ ἐγένετο, 'and there was') to introduce the voice; Peshitta omits this repetition, proceeding directly from the cloud to the voice with a simple conjunction (ܘܩܠܐ, 'and a voice'), reflecting typical Semitic paratactic economy.

Greek uses a feminine participle agreeing with φωνή (λέγουσα, 'saying'); Peshitta uses a masculine relative particle (ܕܐܡܪ, 'that said'), reflecting the masculine gender of ܩܠܐ in Syriac, a routine grammatical concordance difference.

Greek employs a two-word copular construction (οὗτός ἐστιν, 'this is'); Peshitta uses the demonstrative pronoun alone (ܗܢܘ, 'this [is]'), with the copula implicit, a standard Semitic nominal sentence pattern.

Peshitta adds the prepositional phrase ܠܗ ('to him' / 'his'), functioning as an ethical dative or possessive intensifier modifying 'beloved', absent in the Greek witness but reflecting Semitic stylistic preference for pronominal reinforcement.
